key_insight: Academic publishing is seeing a rapid rise in suspicion that manuscripts were produced with generative AI, creating procedural, ethical and trust problems that can harm authors and strain peer review systems.
problem_solved: Identifies and clarifies the challenge of escalating AI-suspicion in submissions — including inconsistent policies, unreliable detection, and damaging false positives — and offers pathways to reduce harm and restore fair review.
method: Survey and synthesis of recent editorial policies, public statements, and reported cases to map the emergence and scale of AI-suspicion.
Analysis of stakeholder perspectives (editors, reviewers, authors) and editorial workflows to locate where suspicion arises and how it is handled.
Evidence-informed recommendations proposing practical policy, disclosure, and review-process changes to limit false accusations and improve transparency.
impact: Helps AI/ML practitioners, journals and institutions adopt fairer, clearer practices so legitimate work isn’t unfairly penalized and peer review remains trustworthy. Provides actionable guidance to balance innovation with integrity in the era of generative models.
visual_elements: Timeline chart of reported AI-suspicion incidents and major publisher policy announcements
Flowchart of editorial decision points showing where AI-suspicion is raised and actions taken
Bar chart or heatmap comparing detection-tool reliability vs. false-positive risk
Stakeholder icons (authors, reviewers, editors, publishers) with callouts summarizing common concerns and recommended actions
paper_title: On the troubling rise of generative AI suspicion in academic publishing
